questions.title: Why did the D.C. Circuit vacate and remand for dismissal for lack of jurisdiction instead of affirming the 12(b)(6) merits dismissal?
questions.question_body: The district court reached the merits (holding OSC misread § 552(a)(4)(F)(i) but still dismissing for failure to state a claim), yet the court of appeals vacated and remanded with instructions to dismiss for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction. Is this because Steel Co. bars assuming jurisdiction to reach the merits? If so, why couldn’t the panel simply affirm on any ground supported by the record? What compels vacatur of the merits ruling when Article III standing is missing?

questions.title: How did the court decide that AFL lacked a concrete injury despite the 'shall ... conduct an investigation' command in 5 U.S.C. § 1216(a)(3)?
questions.question_body: AFL argued it had a procedural right to an OSC investigation under § 1216(a)(3). The panel cites Summers to say a procedural right in vacuo is insufficient. But when a statute uses 'shall,' why doesn’t the failure to perform that nondiscretionary duty itself constitute a cognizable injury? What doctrinal step is the court using to require a further 'concrete and particularized' interest beyond the statutory command?

questions.title: Why isn’t AFL’s asserted informational injury satisfied by § 1216 investigations given Akins and Public Citizen?
questions.question_body: The panel says informational standing requires denial of information that a statute entitles the plaintiff to receive. AFL pointed to the notices and updates available in § 1214 processes and argued § 1216(c) allows similar treatment. The court dismisses this because OSC need not import § 1214’s notice regime into § 1216 matters. Can someone unpack why § 1216(a)(3)’s mandatory investigation language is not itself an entitlement to specific information (as in Akins/Public Citizen)? Is the key that § 1216 lacks a disclosure mandate to the complainant, so no 'entitlement' exists?

questions.title: How did the panel use the 'independent actors' doctrine to find causation and redressability too speculative?
questions.question_body: For AFL’s first theory, the court emphasizes that even if OSC investigated, only a chain of further discretionary decisions (OSC’s enforcement choices, MSPB sanctions, and DOJ’s production) could lead to AFL getting the FOIA records, citing FDA v. AHM and Haaland v. Brackeen. Why is that chain too speculative here? Are there cases where agency investigation or enforcement pressure sufficed for causation/redressability, and what distinguishes those from this context?

questions.title: Why doesn’t a court order compelling an OSC investigation 'very likely' lead to DOJ compliance for redressability purposes?
questions.question_body: The court says redressability turns on how a judgment binds the parties, not on whether its rationale might persuade non-parties (Haaland). But if OSC is ordered to investigate and potentially seek corrective or disciplinary action, wouldn’t that predictably induce DOJ to change its practices? What threshold of likelihood is the D.C. Circuit applying when it rejects this as too speculative under Hecate Energy?

questions.title: What standard of review was applied, and why is it de novo in this procedural posture?
questions.question_body: The opinion states 'our review is de novo,' citing N. Am. Butterfly Ass’n v. Wolf. Is this because the case was dismissed at the pleading stage and standing is a legal question reviewed de novo? Does the same de novo standard apply to both the district court’s interpretation of the statutes and to the Article III standing determination based on the pleadings?

questions.title: Why did the court avoid deciding whether § 552(a)(4)(F)(i) limits OSC’s authority under § 1216?
questions.question_body: The district court decided that § 552(a)(4)(F)(i) does not cabin § 1216 investigations, but the D.C. Circuit expressly did not reach that merits question. Is this purely Steel Co. sequencing (no jurisdiction, no merits)? Or did the unresolved statutory-interpretation dispute bear on standing (e.g., entitlement to information) in a way the court thought unnecessary to decide?

questions.title: How does Heckler v. Chaney factor into a standing analysis rather than just APA reviewability?
questions.question_body: The court cites Chaney to emphasize courts generally may not compel agency enforcement discretion and uses that to undermine causation/redressability. Is the idea that when downstream relief depends on discretionary enforcement choices, a plaintiff cannot show a likely remedy? How is this use of Chaney different from, or overlapping with, the 'committed to agency discretion' bar under the APA?

questions.title: What does the court mean by relaxing imminence/redressability for procedural injuries but 'not injury in fact or causation'?
questions.question_body: The opinion cites Center for Law & Education and Florida Audubon to say procedural-injury cases relax some elements but not injury in fact or causation. Yet it then finds both causation and redressability lacking and also no concrete informational entitlement. How, exactly, are the 'relaxed' requirements supposed to operate here, and why could AFL not satisfy them even under that more forgiving framework?

questions.title: Could AFL have established standing via organizational 'resource-diversion' injury, and why might that fail under D.C. Circuit precedent?
questions.question_body: The opinion doesn’t discuss organizational standing. If AFL had alleged it diverted resources to counteract DOJ’s FOIA practices or OSC’s refusal to investigate, would that suffice? My understanding is that mere litigation expenses don’t count, and the organization must show a perceptible impairment to its non-litigation activities—would that theory be foreclosed here because the injury still depends on independent actors and discretionary enforcement?

questions.title: Would meeting FOIA’s § 552(a)(4)(F)(i) predicates have changed the standing analysis to compel OSC action?
questions.question_body: FOIA says that when a court orders production, awards fees, and questions arbitrary/capricious withholding, OSC 'shall promptly initiate' a disciplinary proceeding. If AFL had those predicates from its separate FOIA suit, would it then have a concrete entitlement sufficient for informational standing, and would redressability be satisfied because the statute makes initiation mandatory? Or would Chaney-like discretion or other hurdles still defeat standing?

questions.title: Is there a narrower form of relief that would have satisfied redressability, such as remanding for OSC to reconsider without the legal error?
questions.question_body: The district court remanded to OSC after finding a legal error but declined to order an investigation. On appeal, the panel says AFL lacks standing altogether. Why wouldn’t a limited APA-style remedy (set aside the legal error and require reconsideration) be enough to show redressability, even if the ultimate decision remains discretionary? Does the lack of any statutory entitlement to notices/information under § 1216 defeat redressability for that narrower relief too?

questions.title: Does separation of powers influence the court’s skepticism about compelling OSC investigations?
questions.question_body: The opinion leans on Chaney and emphasizes limits on compelling agency enforcement choices. Is there an underlying separation-of-powers rationale for treating redressability and causation as weak when judicial relief would steer prosecutorial/investigative discretion? How does that constitutional concern intersect with Article III’s injury and redressability requirements in this case?

questions.title: Does the availability of a direct FOIA remedy under § 552 undermine standing to demand OSC enforcement as an alternative pathway?
questions.question_body: AFL was already litigating FOIA against DOJ and receiving rolling productions. Does the existence of that direct, adequate remedy cut against traceability/redressability for its claim to force OSC to investigate DOJ? Is the court implicitly saying that the proper avenue for the informational injury is the FOIA suit, not collateral enforcement through OSC?

questions.title: Why could the D.C. Circuit raise standing sua sponte and require supplemental briefing, and what factual record governs at this stage?
questions.question_body: Neither party initially addressed standing; the panel ordered supplemental briefing and then dismissed for lack of jurisdiction. Is this because federal courts must ensure Article III standing at all stages? At the motion-to-dismiss posture, are the court’s standing findings constrained to the complaint’s well-pleaded allegations and judicially noticeable materials, or could it consider later developments like DOJ’s rolling FOIA production?
